How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the principal claimant) and his wife XXXX XXXX, citizens of Syria, claim refugee protection pursuant to Sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (IRPA). Background and Allegations
The specifics of the claim are set out in the narrative to the claimants' Personal Information Forms2 (PIFs); the following is a summary.

The claimants have a son who has been granted refugee status in Canada. In 2008 they attempted to come to Canada to visit that son, but were denied visitor visas since immigration officials were not convinced they would return to Syria.3 They were successful in obtaining visitor visas in 2010, and arrived in Canada in XXXX of that year. The following month they filed claims for refugee protection. They claim that they are of Kurdish ethnicity, and that their two politically-active sons were persecuted by the authorities before fleeing the country. The intelligence service allegedly detained and abused the principal claimant because they sought his sons. The claimants fear that, if returned to Syria, they will be harmed or killed by the Syrian authorities. Determination
I find that the claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection. Analysis
The determinative issue in this claim is credibility. Identity
Each claimant's identity as a national of Syria is established by the personal identity documents filed.4

The claimants also claim to be of Kurdish ethnicity, though they have little documentation to support this contention. They did request that a Kurdish interpreter be present at the hearing, but this did not occur, likely due to a scheduling error by the Division. As such, the claimants were not able to demonstrate their ability to speak Kurdish. However, having considered the claimants' request for a Kurdish interpreter and their apparently willingness to testify in Kurdish, the fact that they completed their Personal Information Forms with the help of a Kurdish interpreter, and the fact that they lived in an area of Syria where many Kurds reside, the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimants are of Kurdish ethnicity. Credibility

When a claimant swears that certain facts are true, this creates a presumption that they are indeed true unless there is valid reason to doubt their veracity.5 The determination as to whether a claimant's evidence is credible is made on a balance of probabilities.6

The principal claimant provided most of the oral testimony on behalf of both claimants. The associated claimant testified briefly, though her testimony largely reiterated a portion of her husband's evidence.

The principal claimant was lacking in credibility. He was extremely evasive, and failed to directly answer questions that were put to him as many as three times. When asked about events that had happened to him personally, he tended to provide general answers about the way things are done in Syria. He had considerable difficulty in remembering dates and time periods. However, it was not just the claimant's manner of testifying that raises questions about his credibility, but that testimony itself. Specifically:

Detention of XXXX. The claimants allege that their sons XXXX and XXXX were detained in XXXX of 2004. They were able to locate XXXX at an intelligence facility and to secure his release with a bribe. XXXX eventually fled to Canada and made a successful refugee claim; the claimants disclosed his Personal Information Form7 in support of their own claims. The principal claimant, however, had some difficulty in giving oral testimony that was consistent with his son's PIF.

The principal claimant had considerable difficulty in recounting the dates, or even the months, in which significant events happened. Perhaps more significantly, he had difficulty with some important time periods. He testified that XXXX was detained by intelligence for one week before the claimants paid a bribe for his release. According to the claimants' PIF and that of their son, however, XXXX was in detention from XXXX XXXX, 2004 until XXXX XXXX XXXX 2005-a period of almost ten weeks. The claimant could only explain that he made an error in his testimony, and could not remember the length of the detention, which is not a satisfactory explanation. It is reasonable to expect that, even without recalling exact dates, the claimant would not confuse one week of detention with ten weeks of detention, particularly when his son was allegedly in the hands of Syria's notorious and feared intelligence service.

The principal claimant testified that he paid a bribe of twenty thousand Syrian pounds; he clearly remembered the amount, as he sold some of his property to raise the money. He was reminded that XXXX's PIF describes a bribe of only half that amount,8 but he insisted that he paid twenty thousand.

The claimant was asked to explain how his son was released from detention. He testified that he went to pick XXXX up from the intelligence facility; he located the officer he was to bribe, and XXXX was released to him, and they took a taxi home. This is simply inconsistent with XXXX's PIF, which states that a plainclothes officer took him from his cell, blindfolded him, placed him in a vehicle, and drove him to a location in Aleppo, where he was released and made his way home.9 The claimant could not explain the discrepancy between his testimony and his son's PIF.

The claimants allege that they cannot return to Syria largely because of the political activities of their sons and the problems that resulted from these actions. It is reasonable to expect that the claimants' evidence regarding a key incident would be consistent with their own PIFs and with that of their son XXXX. Their inconsistent and unexplained evidence regarding this matter seriously damages their credibility.

Beatings and bribes. When the claimants first filed their PIFs, there was little indication that the principal claimant had been harmed during his four alleged detentions. His PIF stated that he had been interrogated,10 that food was withheld,11 and that he had to sleep on the floor of his cell.12 At the start of his hearing, the claimants provided a slightly amended PIF narrative, which added the following sentence after a description of the last detention: "As before, I was beaten and mistreated while in custody."13 The claimant then testified that he was repeatedly and viciously tortured by various methods.

The principal claimant was asked why his initial narrative made no mention of such torture, even though he had signed a declaration that the document was complete, true, and correct. He replied that he did indeed mention that he was beaten, tortured, and starved, but the panel notes that this information was not in his initial narrative, nor is it in the information he provided to immigration officials14 when he initiated his claim. Also omitted from the claimants' PIFs is alleged violence suffered by both claimants when the principal claimant was arrested in XXXX of 2010.

The claimants' evidence regarding alleged bribes suffers from the same inconsistency. The principal claimant testified that after he used a bribe to secure XXXXs release in XXXX of 2005, intelligence officials came to his house seeking XXXX XXXX He bribed them and they went away. However, they continued to return every three months, and when he did not have money to bribe them, he was detained. While the claimants' PIFs describe the bribe to release XXXX, and bribes paid in 2008, they simply do not refer to the bribes in 2005. Although asked repeatedly, the principal claimant did not provide an explanation for this omission.

The claimants' PIFs allege that the principal claimant was detained in XXXX of 2010 after intelligence officials demanded money from him but he was unable to pay.15 The principal claimant's oral testimony was different. He claimed that this was one occasion where the intelligence officers did not ask for a bribe, because this matter was so serious that a bribe would not have been accepted, and he did not dare offer one. Although asked repeatedly, the claimant could not provide an explanation for the inconsistency between his oral evidence and his PIF.

All relevant and important facts should be contained in the PIF, and the oral evidence should go on to explain that information.16 The claimants' PIFs omitted important information about alleged torture, and the claimants could not provide a reasonable explanation for this. Their PIFs also omitted important information about bribing intelligence officials, and instead contained apparently false information about another instance of bribery.
The claimants' inconsistent and contradictory evidence on the key issues of torture and bribery further undermines their credibility.

Failure to claim in Cyprus, re-availment to Syria, and delay in departing Syria. One of the claimant's sons, XXXX, made his way to Cyprus, where he made a refugee claim, and the claimants visited him there from XXXX of 2005 to XXXX of 2006.17 Although XXXX's claim was eventually rejected, it was still pending when the claimants visited him. At this point in time, the principal claimant had allegedly been detained twice and severely tortured. Both of his sons had been detained and mistreated for lengthy periods of time, and the intelligence service was allegedly paying regular visits to the claimants' house. Despite this, the claimants did not make a refugee claim in Cyprus, even while visiting their son who himself was a refugee claimant there.

The principal claimant was asked to explain the failure to claim in Cyprus. He testified that they "just didn't" apply, and that they did not know if their son would be accepted as a refugee in Cyprus. This is not a reasonable explanation. Their son had fled alleged persecution, and they too had allegedly experienced persecution. They had no apparent reason to believe that their son would be denied refugee protection by Cyprus, and they would have had little to lose, and much to gain, by filing such claims themselves.

Instead, the claimants returned to Syria, and the principal claimant was asked to explain this. He testified that he hoped his situation would improve, and he was not well-off enough to remain in Cyprus. He had a fear of going back but not a huge fear, and was forced to go back because his wife and mother were ill and his daughters were in Syria. This is not a reasonable explanation. There was little apparent reason for the claimant to expect the situation to improve-the same regime was still in power, and was allegedly seeking his two sons, both of whom had fled the country. The principal claimant had already been detained and tortured because the authorities could not find his sons. In this context, it makes little sense for the claimants to have risked their lives by returning. They would not be able to tend to their daughters or his sick mother if they were detained or killed by the regime.

Not only did the claimants return to Syria, but they made few efforts to leave again, despite allegedly facing continued persecution. They unsuccessfully sought Canadian visas in 2008. They made no other efforts to leave, and did not even think of applying for visas to a European country after their Canadian rejection.

The claimants allege that they fear for their lives in Syria. Their actions are simply inconsistent with this claim. After allegedly experiencing serious persecution, they did not make a claim in Cyprus, despite a lengthy visit there with their son, who himself had claimed asylum. Despite their problems in Syria, they voluntarily returned to that country. Even though they allegedly faced continued persecution, they made few efforts to leave, until they were able to gain entry to Canada.
The claimants' failure to claim in Cyprus, their return to Syria, and their delay in departure further erodes their credibility.

Exit from Syria. Objective evidence indicates that the Syrian regime uses exit controls, and frequently imposes travel bans to prevent certain citizens from leaving the country.18 The claimants allege that they are sought by the feared Syrian intelligence service, and yet they were able to exit the country using their own passports and Canadian visitor visas. The claimants' PIF narratives simply report that they obtained Canadian visas and flew from XXXX to Toronto. In his oral testimony, however, the principal claimant explained that he paid a huge amount of money as a bribe to get out of the airport. When asked why this important information is not in his PIF, the claimant replied that he did not want to disclose this to anybody, and that he did not know this information was important.

The claimant's explanation is not reasonable. When he prepared his PIF, he signed a statement that it was complete, true, and correct. At the outset of the hearing-after counsel made some amendments and additions to the PIFs-both claimants confirmed that the documents were complete, true, and correct. Their omission of important information about their illegal exit from the country seriously damages their credibility.

The claimants are generally lacking in credibility. Even without disbelieving every part of a claimant's testimony, a panel may find the claimant so lacking in credibility that it concludes there is no credible evidence relevant to his claim.19 A claimant's contradictory testimony can cast doubt upon the totality of his oral evidence.20

The claimants were unable to provide consistent evidence about the key elements of their claim. No medical evidence was presented to indicate that the claimants suffer from any condition that might impair their ability to testify or to recall facts and dates, nor was any medical evidence disclosed to corroborate the principal claimant's allegations of torture. The panel recognizes that the claimants are elderly, are not highly educated, testified through the filter of an interpreter, and may have been anxious in the setting of a hearing room. However, these factors are not sufficient to explain the serious deficiencies in their evidence. The claimants' inconsistent and contradictory testimony casts doubt on the totality of their evidence, and the panel finds them so lacking in credibility that there is no credible evidence relevant to their claims, which must therefore fail.

The claimants alleged that they are at risk because of the political activities of their sons. They did not claim that, aside from those activities, they were at risk simply because of their Kurdish ethnicity. However, as the panel has accepted that the claimants are Kurdish-but not the remainder of their evidence-it has also considered whether they would be at risk solely because of their ethnicity.

Objective evidence indicates that Kurds comprise about ten percent of Syria's population. They face discrimination, and are denied the right to learn Kurdish in schools or to celebrate Kurdish festivals.21 They are subject to arrest and imprisonment when they campaign for greater rights.22

The objective evidence clearly establishes that politically-active Kurds are indeed at risk of persecution. That evidence also indicates that as it is not practical for the authorities to detain every political activist, it is largely the more active persons who are arrested.23 Where low-level activists are targeted, the authorities tend to impose short-term detentions, reporting obligations, and monitoring by security forces.24

The claimants do not allege that they are politically active; in fact, they made it clear that they are not. They do not claim that they fear persecution only because they are Kurdish, but because their sons are Kurdish political activists. The panel does not believe their evidence. As such, the panel finds that the claimants are Kurds without any political profile and who have no intention of being politically active. Having carefully considered the evidence, the panel finds that the claimants face no more than a mere possibility of persecution because of their ethnicity.

Finally, the panel notes that conditions in Syria were extremely violent and dangerous at the time of the hearing, as the country appears to be descending into civil war.25 It may well be dangerous for the claimants to return, but any risk they face is a generalized one, faced by the population at large, and therefore the claimants are not persons in need of protection. Conclusion
Each claimant was found to be a citizen of Syria. I found that they have failed to establish their claims with credible or trustworthy evidnce.

For the reasons set out above, I find that XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection, and reject their claims.
